output.title: Why data cleaning is not the whole job
output.body:
Data cleaning helps, but it is only one part of the workflow. If your team still has to categorise rows, route exceptions, or approve cases by hand after the data is clean, you have not removed the manual work. You have only improved the input side.

That is the useful question: not “is the data clean?” but “what still needs human judgment after the data is clean?” In a small business, that usually shows up in the decision layer. A clean record may still need sign-off, a rule applied, or an exception handled. The boring part is that software does not magically know which exceptions you care about.

A practical next step is to map one repeating workflow as input → decision → output. Write down the steps, then mark which ones are rules-based and which ones need judgment or approval. If you want, use a simple time check: how much effort goes into cleaning versus deciding on the cleaned data? Keep that as an estimate, not a benchmark.

If cleaned data still leaves a long tail of manual decisions, that boundary is often where automation fits. Start with the decision layer, not another cleanup tool.
